Focused Question — Does God Deceive? Makr, Judicial Hardening, and Why

A standalone adjudication of the polemic "the God of Islam is the Deceiver," using the dossier's rules — and, by request, with an explicit "why": the reason each theology gives for divine deception/hardening.

1. What the Qur'an says

  • Q 3:54 — "they plotted (makarū) and Allah plotted (makara); and Allah is the best of plotters (khayr al-mākirīn)" (cf. Q 8:30; 27:50; 13:42).
  • Q 4:142 — the hypocrites "think they deceive Allah, but He deceives them."
  • Q 2:15 — "Allah mocks them (yastahziʾu) and prolongs them in their transgression, wandering blindly."
  • Sealing / leading astray: Q 2:7 ("Allah has set a seal on their hearts"); Q 14:4 ("He leaves astray whom He wills and guides whom He wills"); Q 6:110; Q 61:5 ("when they deviated, Allah caused their hearts to deviate").
  • Istidrāj — Q 7:182–183; 68:44: "We will lead them on by degrees whence they know not."

The standard Islamic reading: makr Allāh is counter-plotting / requital — God out-plans those who first plotted evil; "best of plotters" means none escapes His justice. It is not gratuitous lying toward the innocent.

2. What the Bible says (the symmetry)

Structurally identical material — at points more explicit:

  • 1 Kgs 22:20–23 — the LORD sends "a lying spirit in the mouth of all [Ahab's] prophets… 'Go and do so.'"
  • Ezek 14:9 — "if the prophet is deceived… I the LORD have deceived that prophet."
  • 2 Thess 2:11 — "God sends them a strong delusion, that they should believe the lie."
  • Jer 20:7 — "O LORD, You deceived me."
  • Pharaoh: "I will harden Pharaoh's heart" (Exod 4:21; 7:3) — and "Pharaoh hardened his own heart" (Exod 8:15): the same dual causation as Islamic kasb.
  • Isa 6:9–10 (cited by Jesus, Mark 4:12; John 12:40); Rom 1:24,28 ("God gave them up"); Rom 9:18 ("He hardens whom He wills"); Rom 11:8 ("a spirit of stupor").

3. The "why" — the reason each theology gives

This is the heart of the question. Both traditions justify it with the same family of reasons:

ReasonIslamChristianity
Retributive justice (not arbitrary)makr answers their prior makr (Q 3:54); Q 61:5 "when they deviated, He made their hearts deviate""they did not honour God… therefore God gave them over" (Rom 1:21–28); delusion comes "because they refused to love the truth" (2 Thess 2:10–11)
Test / sifting of heartsfitna/ibtilāʾ — "We will surely test you" (Q 2:155; 29:2–3; 47:31)testing and proving (Deut 8:2; 1 Pet 1:7); the parable-veil sifts hearers (Mark 4:11–12)
Just abandonment after repeated refusalistidrāj — the persistent sinner is let to sink (Q 7:182; 6:110)"God gave them up" — withdrawal of restraining grace (Rom 1)
Sovereign wisdom / displayguidance is mercy, not owed; misguidance = withdrawal of an undeserved gift; ḥikma beyond audit"for this purpose I raised you up, to show My power" (Rom 9:17); the potter (Rom 9:20–21)
Mercy as the ultimate aimthe respite of istidrāj still leaves room to repent"God consigned all to disobedience that He may have mercy on all" (Rom 11:32)

So the why is parallel: in mainstream readings the deception/hardening is a judicial response to prior, willful rejection, framed as just requital, a test, and an exercise of sovereign wisdom — never as unprovoked malice toward the innocent. And both preserve human responsibility by dual causation (the person hardens himself and God hardens) and both finally appeal to divine wisdom exceeding human comprehension — the apophatic limit (cap. 09).

4. The internal spectrum — also parallel

How "He leaves astray whom He wills" is reconciled with justice splits each tradition the same way:

  • Mu'tazila (God misguides none unjustly; "misguide" = abandon to one's own choice) ≈ Arminianism (God hardens those who first harden themselves; foreknowledge, conditional).
  • Ashʿarī (God creates all acts; man acquires, kasb) ≈ Calvinism (sovereign decree, reprobation, compatibilist freedom).
  • Māturīdī sits between, like moderate Reformed/Arminian mediations.

The determinism-vs-freedom problem is shared, with mirror-image schools — it is not a defect peculiar to Islam.

Arbiter verdict — does God deceive, and why?

Present. Polemic: "Allah is the Deceiver, so Islam's God is malevolent" (Q 3:54; 4:142). Reply: the texts mean judicial counter-justice, and the Bible says the same thing, sometimes more bluntly.

Weigh.

  • Asymmetric slogan — fails. Ezek 14:9 ("I the LORD have deceived that prophet") and 2 Thess 2:11 are as strong or stronger than Q 3:54. By the symmetry rule (Methodology §3) an argument that, applied evenly, wounds one's own scripture is not usable.
  • The "why" converges. Both give the same justification set: retributive justice, test, just abandonment, sovereign wisdom, ultimate mercy — and both deny gratuitous deception of the innocent.
  • Internal spectrum mirrors. Ashʿarī/Muʿtazila ≈ Calvinist/Arminian: the hard problem is shared, not unique.

Judge.

  • On "is 'God deceives' a charge that distinguishes Islam from Christianity?" — No. The textual and theological structures are symmetric; the polemic fails by symmetry (a clear, nameable result). This is a textbook "knockout" that cancels itself.
  • On "why does God do it?" — both answer identically in kind: judicial requital for prior rejection, within a test, under sovereign wisdom, aimed ultimately at mercy. That answer is internally coherent in each system.
  • On *"is a God who judicially deceives/hardens therefore good or just?" — this is a theodicy / value question, identical* for both scriptures, and the arbiter declines it (Methodology §5): neither tradition gains or loses ground here relative to the other.

Net: the difference is emphasis and vocabulary, not structure — one more "decisive" attack that, held to an even standard, applies to both or to neither.
